label: Def RS
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def RS} \
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item A sequence $(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of elements of a real Banach space $(X, \|\cdot\|)$ is called Schauder basis (of $X$) if for all $x \in X$ there is a unique sequence $(\alpha_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\subset \mathbb{R}$  such that $$x= \sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \alpha_n x_n,$$ where the convergence of the series is to be considered with respect to $\|\cdot \|.$
    \item A Schauder basis $(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of a real Hilbert space $(H, \|\cdot\|)$ is called a Riesz basis (of $H$) if there are  Riesz constants $A\leq B \in (0, \infty)$ such that $$A \|\alpha\|_{\ell_2}^2 = A \sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \alpha_n^2 \leq \left\|\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \alpha_n x_n \right\|^2 \leq B \sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \alpha_n^2 =B \|\alpha\|_{\ell_2}^2$$ holds for all square-summable sequences $\alpha \in \ell_2.$
\end{enumerate}

body_md: Our first result is algebraic: if $\ell_1$ is equipped with the Dirichlet convolution as multiplication, then $\tau\mapsto T_\tau$ is an isomorphism of algebras onto the abelian algebra $\{T_\tau:\tau\in\ell_1\}$ (Theorem~\ref{AlgTtau}). Consequently, if $\tau_1\neq0$ and the Dirichlet inverse $\tau^{-1}$ belongs to $\ell_1$, then $T_\tau$ is invertible with $T_\tau^{-1}=T_{\tau^{-1}}$ (Theorem~\ref{InvTtau}). This connects the question of bases to multiplicative number theory and leads to criteria on $\tau$ that are easy to verify. The following theorem summarises the main consequences.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{MainInformal}
    Let $q\in(1,\infty)$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\tau\in\ell_1$ such that $\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}<2|\tau_1|$, or such that $\tau_1\neq0$ and $\frac1{\tau_1}\tau$ is completely multiplicative. Let $\tau^{-1}$ denote the Dirichlet inverse of $\tau$.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item $\mathcal Z^\tau$ is a Schauder basis of $L_q([0,1]^d)$. If $q=2$, it is a Riesz basis with Riesz constants $A=\|\tau^{-1}\|_{\ell_1}^{-2}$ and $B=\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}^2.$
        \item If $\lambda$ is another sequence with the same properties, with Riesz constants $A_\lambda,B_\lambda$, and $k_0\neq0$, then the mixed system $\{k_0\}\cup\{C^\tau_J,S^\lambda_J:J\in \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}\}$ is a Schauder basis of $L_q([0,1]^d)$, and for $q=2$ a Riesz basis with lower constant $\min\{k_0^2,A,A_\lambda\}$ and upper constant $\max\{k_0^2,B,B_\lambda\}$.
        \item In particular, $\mathcal R_d$ is a Schauder basis of $L_q([0,1]^d)$, and a Riesz basis of $L_2([0,1]^d)$ with Riesz constants $A=\frac23$ and $B=\frac32$, independently of $d$.

name: $d$\textbf{-Dirichlet convolution

label: dDirichlet
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{dDirichlet}
Let $\tau, \lambda: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $a:  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0} \to \mathbb{R}.$ Fix $N \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ and put $\frac N{N_0}:=N_0^{-1}N \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ as well as $a':\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}, \ a'_k:=a_{k \frac N {N_0}}.$
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item It holds $(\tau *_d a)'=(\tau*a')$ and $(\tau*_da)_N=(\tau*a')_{N_0}.$
    \item For all $d \in \mathbb{N}$ the $d$-Dirichlet convolution is pseudo-associative, that is it holds $(\tau * \lambda) *_da=\tau*_d(\lambda*_da).$
    \item It holds $e*_da=a.$
    \item It holds $\tau*_da=0,$ if and only if, it holds $a=0$ or $\tau=0.$
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: \textbf{Properties of the $d$-Dirichlet convolution

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item We have $(\tau *_d a)_k'=(\tau*_da)_{k \frac N {N_0}} = \sum \limits_{j|k} \tau_j a_{\frac k j \frac N {N_0}} = \sum \limits_{j|k}\tau_j a_{\frac k j}'=(\tau*a')_k$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}.$ Further, it holds $(\tau*_da)_N = \sum \limits_{k|N_0} \tau_k a_{\frac {N_0} k \frac N {N_0}}=\sum \limits_{k|N_0} \tau_k a'_{\frac{N_0} k}=(\tau*a')_{N_0}.$                                                                                                                                                                                  
    \item We use the associativity of $*$. Let $N \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$, then it holds $$((\tau*\lambda)*_da)_N= ((\lambda*\tau)*a')_{N_0}=(\lambda*(\tau*a'))_{N_0}=(\lambda*(\tau*_da)')_{N_0}=(\lambda*_d(\tau*_da))_N.$$
    \item For any $N \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ we calculate $(e*_da)_N=(e*a')_{N_0}=(a')_{N_0}=a_N$.
    \item For the if part we calculate $(0*_da)_N=(0*a')_{N_0}=0$ as well as $(\tau*_d0)_N=(\tau*0')_{N_0}=(\tau*0)_{N_0}=0$. Regarding the only if part let $\tau \neq 0.$ For any $N \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ we have $0=0'=(\tau*_da)'=(\tau*a'),$ showing $a'=0$ and in particular $0=a_{N_0}'=a_N.$
\end{enumerate}

label: Ttau
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Ttau}
    Let $q \in (1,\infty), \ d \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\tau \in \ell_1.$ Consider the operator $T_\tau$ from \eqref{DefTtau}.  Then it holds:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item $T_\tau$ is a well-defined linear operator and bounded, where $\|T_\tau\|\leq\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}.$
        \item Assume additionally $\|\tau\|_{\ell_1} < 2|\tau_1|,$ then $T_\tau$ is bijective and it holds $\|T_\tau^{-1}\| \leq \frac{1}{2|\tau_1|-\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}}.$
        \item Assume $\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}<2|\tau_j|$ for some $j \in \mathbb{N},$ then $T_\tau$ is bijective onto a closed subspace and $\|T_\tau^{-1}\| \leq \frac 1 {2|\tau_j|-\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}}$.
        \item Let $h,f \in L_q([0,1])$ such that $T_\tau h = f,$ then $T_\tau (h_\alpha) = f_\alpha$ holds for all $\alpha \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}.$ 
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: \textbf{Sum and scale operators $T_\tau$

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item Put $I:=[0,1]^d.$ For each $g \in L_q(I)$ it holds \begin{equation}\label{1} \|G_k g\|_q^q =\int_I |g(kx)|^q \ \mathrm d x = \frac 1 {k^d} \int_{[0,k]^d} |g(x)|^q \ \mathrm d x = \frac 1 {k^d} \sum \limits_{j \in \{0, ..., k-1\}^d} \int_{j+I} |g(x)|^q \ \mathrm d x =\int_I |g(x)|^q \ \mathrm d x =\|g\|_q^q \end{equation} and consequently $$\|T_\tau g\|_q \leq \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty |\tau_k| \|g\|_q = \|\tau\|_{\ell_1} \|g\|_q.$$ In particular, $T_\tau$ is a well-defined linear operator bounded by $\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}.$
    \item Using (i), we set $\kappa=\tau - (\tau_1, 0,0, ...) \in \ell_1$ and derive $$\|T_\tau-\tau_1 \text{Id}\| = \|T_\kappa\| \leq \|\kappa\|_{\ell_1}=\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}-|\tau_1|<|\tau_1|.$$ Now $T_\tau= \tau_1 \text{Id} - (\tau_1 \text{Id}-T_\tau)$ is boundedly invertible by \cite[Ex. 5.7.1]{AppliedFuncAna} and from the proof in combination with \cite[Prop 3.4]{FuncAnaAppl} we arrive at the estimate $$ \|T_\tau^{-1}\| \leq \frac 1{|\tau_1|- \|T_\tau-\tau_1 \text{Id}\|} \leq \frac{1}{2|\tau_1|-\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}}.$$
    \item Due to \eqref{1} we calculate that $$\|T_\tau g\|_{L_q([0,1]^d)} \geq |\tau_j| \|g\|_{L_q([0,1]^d)} - \sum \limits_{k=1, k \neq j}^\infty |\tau_k| \|g\|_{L_q([0,1]^d)} = (2|\tau_j|-\|\tau\|_{\ell_1})\|g\|_{L_q([0,1]^d)}$$ holds for all $g \in L_q([0,1]^d).$ This shows injectivity and $\|T_\tau^{-1}\| \leq (2|\tau_j|-\|\tau\|_{\ell_1})^{-1},$ where $T_\tau^{-1}$ is to be understood as the inverse of $T_\tau: L_q([0,1]^d) \to \operatorname{ran}(T_\tau).$                                                                                                                                                                                     

    Regarding closedness of the image, let $y_n=T_\tau x_n$ be a sequence converging to $y \in L_q([0,1]^d),$ then $(y_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a Cauchy sequence. It follows $\|x_n-x_m\|=\|T_\tau^{-1}(y_n-y_m)\| \leq \|T_\tau^{-1}\|\|y_n-y_m\| \to 0$ if $n,m \to \infty.$ Whence $(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is itself a Cauchy sequence and converges to some $x \in L_q([0,1]^d).$ Continuity of $T_\tau$ shows $y=T_\tau x \in \text{ran}(T_\tau).$ 
    \item For all $x \in I$ it holds $$T_\tau (h_\alpha)(x)=\sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \tau_k h_\alpha(kx)=\sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \tau_kh(\alpha^T(kx)) = \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \tau_k h(k(\alpha^Tx)) = T_\tau h (\alpha^Tx) = f(\alpha^Tx) = f_\alpha(x).$$
\end{enumerate}

label: AlgTtau
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{AlgTtau}

Let $\mathcal A:=\{T_\tau: \tau \in \ell_1\} \subset \mathcal L(L_q([0,1]^d),$ then $\mathcal A$ is an abelian sub-algebra of $\mathcal L(L_q([0,1]^d).$ Further, the map $A: \ell_1 \to \mathcal A$, $\tau \mapsto T_{\tau}$, is an isomorphism of algebras with $\|A\|=1,$ if $\ell_1$ is equipped with the Dirichlet convolution as multiplication.
head: environment
name: \textbf{Algebraic structure of $\{T_\tau:\tau \in \ell_1\}$

label: Submult
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\tau, \lambda \in \ell_1.$ Clearly, for any $k \in \mathbb{R}$ we have $T_\tau + k T_\lambda = T_{\tau + k \lambda} \in \mathcal A,$ showing that $\mathcal A$ is a subspace and $A$ is linear. We will now prove that $\tau * \lambda \in \ell_1$ and $T_\tau \circ T_\lambda=T_{\tau*\lambda}$. It holds \begin{equation} \label{Submult}
    \|a*b\|_{\ell_1}=\sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty |(a*b)_k| \leq \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \sum \limits_{\substack{c,d \in \mathbb{N} \\ cd=k}}|a_c| |b_d| = \left(\sum \limits_{c=1}^\infty |a_c|\right) \left(\sum \limits_{d=1}^\infty |b_d|\right) = \|a\|_{\ell_1}\|b\|_{\ell_1},
\end{equation} whence $\ell_1$ is closed under multiplication.                                                                   

                                                                                                                                                                                                          
From \eqref{1} it follows that $G_k$ is an isometry for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, whence $\|G_k\|=1.$ Obviously $G_k \circ G_j=G_{kj}$ holds and we obtain $$ T_\tau \circ T_\lambda = \left(\sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \tau_k G_k\right) \circ \left(\sum \limits_{j=1}^\infty \lambda_j G_j\right) = \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \sum \limits_{j=1}^\infty \tau_k \lambda_j G_{kj}.$$ The  series on the right hand side converges absolutely because of $\sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \sum \limits_{j=1}^\infty |\tau_k| |\lambda_j|= \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty |\tau_k| \|\lambda\|_{\ell_1} = \|\tau\|_{\ell_1} \|\lambda\|_{\ell_1}.$ Thus, we may rearrange this expression to $\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \left(\sum \limits_{\substack{j,k \in \mathbb{N}: \\ jk=n}} \tau_k \lambda_j\right)G_n = \sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty (\tau*\lambda)_n G_n= T_{\tau * \lambda}.$ 
In particular, because $*$ is commutative it follows $T_\tau \circ T_\lambda=T_{\tau*\lambda}=T_{\lambda*\tau}=T_\lambda \circ T_\tau$ and $\mathcal A$ is an abelian sub-algebra.

We have already seen that $\|T_\tau\| \leq \|\tau_1\|_{\ell_1}$ holds for all $\tau \in \ell_1,$ showing that $\|A\| \leq 1.$ Because $\|T_e\|=\|\text{Id}\|=1$ and $\|e\|_{\ell_1}=1,$ we get $\|A\| \geq 1$ and whence $\|A\|=1.$                                                                                                 

It is clear that $A$ is a surjective homomorphism of algebras. In order to prove injectivity let $v:=(1,...,1)$ be the vector of ones, then $kv=(k,...,k)$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}.$ We notice that $T_\tau(\cos(2 \pi v^T\cdot))=\sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \tau_k \cos( 2 \pi (kv)^T\cdot),$ hence $\int_{[0,1]^d} \cos(2 \pi (kv)^Tx) T_\tau(\cos(2 \pi v^T\cdot)) \mathrm d x=\frac{\tau_k} 2.$ Now $T_\tau=T_\lambda$ implies $$\tau_k=2\int_{[0,1]^d} \cos(2 \pi (kv)^Tx) T_\tau(\cos(2 \pi v^T\cdot)) \mathrm d x=2\int_{[0,1]^d} \cos(2 \pi (kv)^Tx) T_\lambda(\cos(2 \pi v^T\cdot)) \mathrm d x=\lambda_k$$                            
for all $k \in \mathbb{N},$ which in turn implies $\tau=\lambda$ and proves that $A$ is injective and consequently bijective.

label: InvTtau
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: \textbf{Invertibility of }$T_\tau$

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item First let $\tau_0=0,$ then $T_\tau(1)=0=T_\tau(0)$ and $T_\tau$ is not injective. Thus, assume $\tau_0 \neq 0.$
    
    Let $h \in \ker(T_\tau),$ that is, $h \in L_q([0,1]^d)$ with $T_\tau(h)=0.$ We write $h=h_0 +\sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}}a_J \sqrt 2 c_J + b_J \sqrt 2 s_J$ from which $$0=T_\tau h = \tau_0 h_0 + \sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} (\tau *_d a)_J \sqrt 2 c_J + (\tau *_d b)_J \sqrt 2 s_J$$ and $\tau *_d a=0_{ \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}}=\tau *_d b$ as well as $\tau_0 h_0=0$ follow. See Proposition \ref{Coeff}(i) below for a detailed proof of these formulae.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
    This implies $h_0=\frac {\tau_0 h_0}{\tau_0}=0$ as well as $a=0=b$ because $\tau \neq 0.$ We conclude $h=0,$ whence $\ker(T_\tau)=\{0\}$ and consequently shows that $T_\tau$ is injective.                                                                                                                             
    \item It holds $T_{\tau^{-1}} \in \mathcal L(L_q([0,1]^d))$ and $T_\tau \circ T_{\tau^{-1}}=T_e=\text{Id}=T_{\tau^{-1}} \circ T_\tau.$
\end{enumerate}

label: DirichletNeumann
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{DirichletNeumann}
    Given $\tau \in \ell_1$ with $\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}<2|\tau_1|$ we used the Neumann series           
    in Theorem \ref{Ttau}(ii) to prove that $T_\tau$ is bijective. We will now show that under this condition the Dirichlet inverse of $\tau$ is summable and $\|\tau^{-1}\|_{\ell_1} \leq \frac 1 {2|\tau_1|-\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}}$. 
    
    Because $|\tau_1|>\frac{\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}}{2} \geq 0$ we know that $\tau_1 \neq 0$ and that the           
    Dirichlet inverse must exist. It holds $$\tau=\tau_1 \cdot e-(\tau_1 \cdot e-\tau) = \tau_1 \cdot (e-(e-\tau_1^{-1} \cdot \tau)).$$ Further, $\|e-\tau_1^{-1}\cdot\tau\|_{\ell_1}=|\tau_1^{-1}| \|\tau_1e-\tau\|_{\ell_1}=\frac{\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}-|\tau_1|}{|\tau_1|}<1$ holds true. For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\tau:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ we write $\tau^{*n}:=\tau * \tau * ... * \tau$ where the right hand side consists of $n$ factors and $\tau^{*0}=e.$ Because of \eqref{Submult} it holds $\|\kappa^{*n}\|_{\ell_1} \leq \|\kappa\|^n_{\ell_1}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ and $\kappa \in \ell_1.$ Since $\ell_1$ is complete, the series $\tau_1^{-1} \sum \limits_{n=0}^\infty (e-\tau_1^{-1} \cdot \tau)^{*n}$ converges in $\ell_1$ and it is bounded by $|\tau_1^{-1}| \sum \limits_{n=0}^\infty \|e-\tau_1^{-1} \cdot \tau\|^n_{\ell_1} \leq |\tau_1^{-1}|\sum \limits_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}-|\tau_1|}{|\tau_1|}\right)^n=\frac 1 {|\tau_1|} \frac 1 {1-\frac{\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}-|\tau_1|}{|\tau_1|}}=\frac 1 {2|\tau_1|-\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}}.$ 
    One can now proceed as in \cite[Ex. 5.7.1]{AppliedFuncAna}                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
    in order to see that the limit is in fact the Dirichlet inverse.

                                                                                                                                       

    More interestingly the equation                                                                                  
    $\tau^{-1}=\tau_1^{-1} \sum \limits_{n=0}^\infty (e-\tau_1^{-1} \cdot \tau)^{*n}$ holds true in a more general sense for all $\tau:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ as long as $\tau_1 \neq 0.$ Letting $S_m := \tau_1^{-1} \sum \limits_{n=0}^m(e-\tau_1^{-1}\tau)^{*n}$ it holds $S_m \to \tau^{-1}$ pointwise. To see this we calculate $$\tau S_m=S_m \tau = S_m(\tau_1 \cdot (e-(e-\tau_1^{-1} \cdot \tau)))=e-(e-\tau_1^{-1} \tau)^{*(m+1)}.$$ Now we prove $(e-\tau_1^{-1}\tau)^{*m}_k=0$ for all $1 \leq k \leq m$ inductively. The case $m=1$ is clear.                                                              
    Assuming the statement is true for $m \in \mathbb{N}$ we calculate $$(e-\tau_1^{-1}\tau)^{*(m+1)}_k=((e-\tau_1^{-1}\tau)^{*m}*(e-\tau_1^{-1}\tau))_k = \sum \limits_{j|k}(e-\tau_1^{-1}\tau)^{*m}_j (e-\tau_1^{-1}\tau)_{\frac k j}.$$
    First let $k \leq m,$ then because of $j \leq k \leq m$ for every divisor $j$ of $k,$ we get $(e-\tau_1^{-1}\tau)^{*m}_j=0$ and the right hand side sum vanishes. Similarly in case $k=m+1$ all summands vanish, except possibly             
    $j=k=m+1.$ But then $(e-\tau_1^{-1}\tau)_1=0.$ From this we see the pointwise convergence of $S_m$ as well as the limit being $\tau^{-1}.$

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Basiscrit}
    Let $q \in (1,\infty), d \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\tau \in \ell_1.$
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item Let $\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}<2|\tau_1|,$ then $\mathcal Z^\tau$ is a Schauder basis of $L_q([0,1]^d).$ If $q=2$ it is a Riesz basis with Riesz constants $A=\frac 1 {\|\tau^{-1}\|_{\ell_1}^2} \geq (2|\tau_1|-\|\tau\|_{\ell_1})^2$ and $B=\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}^2.$

        =\frac{|\tau_1|^4}{\|\mu \cdot \tau\|_{\ell_1}^2} \geq\frac{|\tau_1|^4}{\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}^2}$ and $B=\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}^2,$ where $\mu$ is the Möbius function.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Basis criteria

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item This follows from the combination of Lemma \ref{ZystemSRBasis}(ii), Remark \ref{DirichletNeumann} and Theorem \ref{Ttau}(ii) and (iii).
        \item By \cite[Thm. 2.17]{Numertheory} the Dirichlet inverse of $\frac 1 {\tau_1} \cdot \tau$ is given by $\mu \cdot \frac 1 {\tau_1} \cdot \tau,$ therefore we may calculate the inverse of $\tau$ via $\tau^{-1}=(\tau_1 \cdot \frac 1 {\tau_1} \cdot \tau)^{-1}=\frac 1 {\tau_1^2} \cdot \mu \cdot \tau,$ for which it holds $$\|\tau^{-1}\|_{\ell_1}= \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac 1 {|\tau_1|^2} \cdot |\mu_k| \cdot |\tau_k| = \frac 1 {|\tau_1^2|} \|\mu \cdot \tau\|_{\ell_1} \leq \frac 1 {|\tau_1|^2} \|\tau\|_{\ell_1}< \infty$$ because $\mu$ is bounded by 1. Whence, $\tau$ and $\tau^{-1}$ are summable. By Theorem \ref{InvTtau}(ii) the operator $T_\tau$ is bijective and $T_\tau^{-1}=T_{\tau^{-1}}$ gives $\|T_\tau^{-1}\|\leq \|\tau^{-1}\|_{\ell_1} = \frac{\|\mu \cdot \tau\|_{\ell_1}}{|\tau_1|^2} \leq \frac{\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}}{|\tau_1|^2}.$ The rest follows from Lemma \ref{ZystemSRBasis}(ii).
    \end{enumerate}

    \item $\tau_1\neq0$ and the Dirichlet inverse $\tau^{-1}$ belongs to $\ell_1$.
\end{enumerate}
In case either assertion holds true the operator $T_\tau:L_q([0,1]^d) \to L_q([0,1]^d)$ is bijective with $T_\tau^{-1}=T_{\tau^{-1}}$, $\mathcal Z^\tau$ is a Schauder basis of $L_q([0,1]^d)$, and for $q=2$ it is a Riesz basis with Riesz constants $A=\|\tau^{-1}\|_{\ell_1}^{-2}$ and $B=\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}^2$.

name: \textbf{A Wiener-type basis criterion

title: Proof
body_md: The equivalence of (i) and (ii) is \cite[Thm. 1]{HewittWilliamson1957}. Note that the inverse in $\ell_1$ is the Dirichlet inverse, which is real if $\tau$ is real, and that $\tau_1\neq0$ is equivalent to its existence. If (ii) holds, Theorem \ref{InvTtau}(ii) shows that $T_\tau$ is bijective with $T_\tau^{-1}=T_{\tau^{-1}}$. By Lemma \ref{ZystemSRBasis}(ii), $\mathcal Z^\tau$ is a Schauder basis of $L_q([0,1]^d)$ and for $q=2$ a Riesz basis with constants $\|T_\tau^{-1}\|^{-2}$ and $\|T_\tau\|^2$. Since $\|T_\tau\|\leq\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}$ and $\|T_\tau^{-1}\|=\|T_{\tau^{-1}}\|\leq\|\tau^{-1}\|_{\ell_1}$ by Theorem \ref{Ttau}(i), the constants $A=\|\tau^{-1}\|_{\ell_1}^{-2}$ and $B=\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}^2$ are admissible.

title: Remark
body_md:
{\textbf{(Repeated transforms of $\mathcal Z^\tau$).}}
    In order to obtain Riesz and Schauder bases of the Lebesgue spaces we chose the orthonormal basis $\mathcal Z^e= \{1\} \cup \{\sqrt 2 \cos(2 \pi J^T\cdot), \sqrt 2 \sin(2 \pi J^T \cdot): J \in           
     \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}\}$ as a starting point and transformed this system using a bijective operator $T_\tau$ resulting in the system $\mathcal Z^\tau.$ Since Riesz and Schauder bases also are suitable starting points for a transformation, one might consider to transform $\mathcal Z^\tau$ again with another bijective operator $T_\lambda$ in order to achieve new systems unobtainable from $\mathcal Z^e$ in a single transformation. However, due to Theorem \ref{AlgTtau} this           
    is not necessary as the transformation of $\mathcal Z^\tau$ with $T_\lambda$ results in the transformation of $\mathcal Z^e$ with the map $T_{\tau*\lambda}.$ However, additional restrictions like $2|\tau_1|>\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}$ may be easier met by an application of multiple operators rather than a single composite operator.

label: SurjTtau
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{SurjTtau}
    Let $q \in (1,\infty), d \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\tau \in \ell_1.$ Let $T_\tau:L_q([0,1]^d) \to L_q([0,1]^d)$ be surjective, then $\mathcal Z^\tau$ is a Schauder basis of $L_q([0,1]^d)$ and it holds $\tau_1 \neq 0 \neq \tau_0.$
head: environment
name: \textbf{Surjectivity of $T_\tau$

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $\tau_0=0.$ Any $f \in L_q([0,1]^d)$ can be written as $f=f_0+\sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} a_J \sqrt 2 c_J + b_J \sqrt 2 s_J$ for some $a,b: \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0} \to \mathbb{R}.$ According to Proposition \ref{Coeff}(i) it holds $T_\tau f = \sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} (\tau*_da)_J \sqrt 2 c_J + (\tau*_db)_J \sqrt 2 s_J,$ whence 1 is not in the image of $T_\tau,$ a contradiction to $T_\tau$ being surjective.           
    If $\tau_0\neq 0$, it follows from Theorem \ref{InvTtau}(i)  that $T_\tau$ is injective and consequently bijective. From Lemma \ref{ZystemSRBasis}(ii) we infer that $\mathcal Z^\tau$ is a Schauder basis. Now assume $\tau_1=0$ and consider $g=\sqrt 2c_\textbf{1}.$ Because $\mathcal Z^\tau$ is a Schauder basis we may write $g=g_0 \tau_0+\sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} a_J C^\tau_J + b_J S^\tau_J,$ where $g_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $a,b: \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0} \to \mathbb{R}.$ Using Proposition \ref{Coeff}(ii) we calculate $b=0$ and from $0=\int_{[0,1]^d}g(x) \mathrm d x = g_0 \tau_0$ we see $g_0=0.$ Using that $g$ is bounded we arrive at the contradiction \begin{align*}
        1=\int_{[0,1]^d} g(x) g(x) \mathrm d x = \sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} a_J \int_{[0,1]^d} g(x) C_J^\tau(x) \mathrm d x = \sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} \sum \limits_{k=2}^\infty a_J \tau_k \int_{[0,1]^d} \sqrt 2 c_\textbf{1}(x) \sqrt 2 c_{kJ}(x) \mathrm d x = 0,
    \end{align*} because $kJ \neq \textbf{1}$ holds for all $k \in \mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}$ and $J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ according to Lemma \ref{kJ=N}. Whence $\tau_1 \neq 0.$

label: Hilbert
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Hilbert}
    Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\tau \in \ell_1.$ If $T_\tau:L_2([0,1]^d) \to L_2([0,1]^d)$ is surjective, then $$\bigg\{a \in \ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}):\sum \limits_{i=1}^\infty a_{iJ} \tau_i = 0 \text{ for all } J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0} \bigg\}=\{0\}.$$
head: environment
name: \textbf{The Hilbert case

title: Proof
body_md: Let $a \in \ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})$ such that $\sum \limits_{i=1}^\infty a_{iJ} \tau_i = 0 \text{ for all } J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$. Then $f:= \sum \limits_{K \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}}^\infty a_K \sqrt 2 c_K$ converges in $L_2([0,1]^d).$ Further, we  calculate $$\int_{[0,1]^d} f(x) C^\tau_J(x) \mathrm d x = \sum \limits_{K \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}}^\infty \sum \limits_{i=1}^\infty a_K \tau_i \int_{[0,1]^d} \sqrt 2 c_K(x) \sqrt 2 c_{iJ}(x) \mathrm d x= \sum \limits_{i=1}^\infty a_{iJ} \tau_i=0$$ as well as $\int_{[0,1]^d} f(x) \mathrm d x=0=\int_{[0,1]^d} f(x) S^\tau_J(x) \mathrm d x.$ Thus, $f=0$ and $a=0$ follow.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The case $q \neq 2$ can be studied in a similar fashion.          
     Let $T_\tau:L_q([0,1]^d)\rightarrow L_q([0,1]^d)$  be surjective.                                                           
     Using the Hahn-Banach theorem and the characterisation of the dual space of $L_q([0,1]^d)$, one sees that the only $f \in L_{q'}([0,1]^d)$ such that $\int_{[0,1]^d} f(x) \mathrm d x=\int_{[0,1]^d} f(x) S^\tau_J(x) \mathrm d x=\int_{[0,1]^d} f(x) C^\tau_J(x) \mathrm d x=0$ for all $J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ is the zero function. Here, $q'=         
     \frac{q}{q-1} \in (1,\infty)$ is the dual exponent. Since $\mathcal Z^e$ is a Schauder basis of $L_{q'}([0,1]^d)$ we can do an analogous calculation as before, however, one does not know which sequences to check because this depends on the convergence of the corresponding series in $L_{q'}([0,1]^d).$

label: ellhat
title: Proposition
body_md:
{\color{blue}{\label{ellhat}}}
Let $$\hat\ell_d :=\left\{\tau: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R} \vert \                                                                        
\exists c=c(\tau) \in [0,\infty) \text{ such that } \|\tau*_da\|_{\ell_2} \leq c \|a\|_{\ell_2} \          
\forall\, a \in \ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})\right\}$$ and let $\|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d}$ be the infimum of all such $c.$ 

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $(\hat\ell_d,\|\cdot\|_{\hat\ell_d})$ is a normed algebra, $\|\cdot\|_{\hat\ell_d}$ is sub-multiplicative, that is $\|\tau*\mu\|_{\hat\ell_d} \leq \|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d} \|\mu\|_{\hat\ell_d}$ for all $\tau, \mu \in \hat\ell_d$ and we have the embeddings $\ell_1 \hookrightarrow \hat\ell_d \hookrightarrow \ell_2.$                                 
$\hat \ell_d$ is commutative and unital with unit $e$ and $\|e\|_{\hat \ell_d}=1$.
\item Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, then $$S_\tau: L_2([0,1]^d)_0 \to L_2([0,1]^d)_0, \sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} a_J \sqrt 2 c_J + b_J \sqrt 2 s_J \mapsto \sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} (\tau *_d a)_J \sqrt 2 c_J + (\tau *_d b)_J \sqrt 2 s_J$$ is a well-defined and bounded linear operator if, and only if, $\tau \in \hat\ell_d$ holds, in which case $\|S_\tau\|=\|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d}$ holds true. $S_\tau$ is bijective if, and only if, $\tau_1 \neq 0$ and $\tau^{-1} \in \hat\ell_d$ holds, where $\tau^{-1}$ is the Dirichlet inverse, in which case $S_\tau^{-1}=S_{\tau^{-1}}$ holds true.
\item Given $\tau \in \ell_2$ define $C^\tau, S^\tau$ as in \eqref{Funktionentau}, then $C^\tau_J, S^\tau_J \in L_2([0,1]^d)$ for all $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and $J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}.$ Define $\mathcal{Z}^\tau_0:=\mathcal Z^\tau \backslash \{\tau_0\},$                                                                                                                                                          
then                                  
is a Riesz basis of $L_2([0,1]^d)_0$ if, and only if,                    
$\tau_1\neq 0$ and $\tau, \tau^{-1} \in \hat\ell_d.$ The optimal Riesz constants in this case are $A=\|\tau^{-1}\|_{\hat\ell_d}^{-2}$ and $B=\|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d}^2.$
\item The operator $S: \hat\ell_d \to \{S_\tau: \tau \in \hat\ell_d\}, \ \tau \mapsto S_\tau$ is an          
isometric isomorphism and an isomorphism of algebras.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: \textbf{The sequence spaces} $\hat\ell_d$

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Let $\tau, \lambda \in \hat\ell_d$ and choose $c(\tau), c(\lambda)$ as in the definition of $         
\hat\ell_d.$ For all $a \in \ell_2$ it holds                                                                                                    
$$\|(\tau+\lambda)*_da\|_{\ell_2}=\|\tau*_da+\lambda*_da\|_{\ell_2} \leq \|\tau*_da\|_{\ell_2}+\|\lambda*_da\|_{\ell_2} \leq (c(\tau)+c(\lambda))\|a\|_{\ell_2},$$ 
whence $\tau+\lambda \in \hat\ell_d$ and taking the infimum yields $\|\tau + \lambda\|_{\hat\ell_d}\leq \|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d}+\|\lambda\|_{\hat\ell_d}.$ Scalar multiples and absolute homogeneity can be addressed similarly. From $\|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d}=0$ it follows $0 \leq \|\tau*a\|_{\ell_2} \leq 0 \|a\|_{\ell_2}=0$ and $\|\tau\|_{\ell_2}=\|\tau*a\|_{\ell_2}=0$, which implies $\tau*_da=0$ for all $a \in \ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})$ and shows $\tau=0$ by \ref{dDirichlet}(iv). All remaining properties of vector spaces, norms and the multiplication are immediately seen to hold true. 

Let $\tau, \mu \in \hat\ell_d$ and $a \in \ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}),$ then $\|(\tau*\mu)*_da\|_{\ell_2}=\|\tau*_d(\mu*_da)\|_{\ell_2} \leq \|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d} \|\mu*_da\|_{\ell_2} \leq \|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d} \|\mu\|_{\hat\ell_d} \|a\|_{\ell_2}$ shows $\tau*\mu \in \hat\ell_d$ and $\|\tau*\mu\|_{\hat\ell_d} \leq \|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d} \|\mu\|_{\hat\ell_d}.$ The embedding $\ell_1 \hookrightarrow \hat\ell_d$ follows from Theorem \ref{Ttau}(i) and Proposition \ref{Coeff}. The embedding $\hat\ell_d \hookrightarrow \ell_2$ follows from $\|\tau\|_{\ell_2} = \|\tau*_da\|_{\ell_2} \leq \|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d} \|a\|_{\ell_2}=\|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_d},$ where $a_{(1,...,1)}=1$ and $a_J=0$ for all $J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0} \backslash \{(1,...,1)\}$.
\item The first part follows immediately from the definition of $\hat\ell_d, S_\tau$ and $\mathcal Z^e \backslash \{1\}$ being an orthonormal basis of $L_2([0,1]^d)_0.$ If $\tau_1 \neq 0$ and $\tau^{-1} \in \hat\ell_d,$ then clearly $S_\tau^{-1}=S_{\tau^{-1}}.$ Let $S_\tau$ be bijective, then one can proceed as in Lemma \ref{SurjTtau} to see $\tau_1 \neq 0.$ Let $g=\sum \limits_{J\in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} a_J \sqrt 2 c_J + b_J \sqrt 2 s_J$ be any element of $L_2([0,1]^d)_0$.                
Then the coefficients form a square-summable sequence. Because $S_\tau$ is surjective, there is another element $f=\sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} \alpha_J \sqrt 2 c_J + \beta_J \sqrt 2 s_J,$ where the coefficients again form a square-summable sequence, such that $S_\tau f=g.$ This shows $\tau*_d\alpha=a$ and $\tau*_d\beta=b,$ from which $\alpha=\tau^{-1}*_da$ and $\beta=\tau^{-1}*_db$ follow. In particular, because any square-summable sequence can be chosen as the coefficients of $g,$ this shows $\tau^{-1}*_da \in \ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})$ for all $a \in \ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})$                                                                                                                                                             
and that the inverse is given by $$S_\tau^{-1}: L_2([0,1]^d)_0 \to L_2([0,1]^d)_0, \quad \sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} a_J \sqrt 2 c_J + b_J \sqrt 2 s_J \mapsto \sum \limits_{J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}} (\tau^{-1} *_d a)_J \sqrt 2 c_J + (\tau^{-1} *_d b)_J \sqrt 2 s_J,$$ which means $S_\tau^{-1}=S_{\tau^{-1}}.$ By the open mapping theorem, $S_\tau^{-1}=S_{\tau^{-1}}$ is bounded, implying $\tau^{-1} \in \hat\ell_d.$ 

\item The first part follows from $         
\mathcal Z^e_0:=\mathcal Z^e \backslash \{1\}$ being an orthonormal basis of the Hilbert space $L_2([0,1]^d)_0,$                
since the coefficients are in $\ell_2.$ Further, $S_\tau$ maps the elements of $         
\mathcal Z^e_0$ to those of $\mathcal Z^\tau_0.$                               
By \cite[Ch.3]{Basen} it follows that $\mathcal Z^\tau_0$               
is a Riesz basis of $L_2([0,1]^d)_0$ if, and only if, $S_\tau$ is bijective and $S_\tau, S_\tau^{-1}=S_{\tau^{-1}}$ are bounded.          
The rest follows from (ii),          
in particular, that the optimal Riesz constants in this case are $B=\|S_\tau\|^2=\|\tau\|^2_{\hat\ell_d}$ and $A=\|S_\tau^{-1}\|^{-2}=\|\tau^{-1}\|^{-2}_{\hat\ell_d}.$
\item $S$ being an isomorphism of algebras follows from $*_d$ being pseudo-associative, see          
Lemma \ref{dDirichlet}(ii), and bilinear. Clearly, $S$ is surjective and an isometric isomorphism by (ii), from which injectivity and consequently bijectivity follow. 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
\end{enumerate}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ellhatd}
   It holds $\hat \ell_d = \hat \ell_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_{\hat \ell_1} = \|\cdot\|_{\hat \ell_d}$ for all $d \in \mathbb{N}.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $P_d:=\{J\in \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}:\gcd(J_1,\dots,J_d)=1\}$ denote the set of primitive vectors in $ \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$. Every $K\in \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ can be written uniquely as $K=nJ$ with $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $J\in P_d$, namely $n=\gcd(K_1,\dots,K_d)$ and $J=\frac1nK$. Moreover, if $J\in P_d$, $k,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $M\in \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ satisfy $kM=nJ$, 
                                                                                         
then $M=\frac nkJ$ by Lemma \ref{kJ=N}, since $(nJ)_0=n$ for $J\in P_d$. 
                                                                        
Let $\tau \in \hat \ell_d$ and $a \in \ell_2.$ Pick $J=(1,\dots,1)\in P_d$ and define $b: \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $b_{kJ}:=a_k$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $b_M:=0$ else. Then $b\in\ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})$ with $\|b\|_{\ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})}=\|a\|_{\ell_2}$, and by the above
$$(\tau*a)_n=\sum \limits_{k|n} \tau_k a_{\frac n k} = \sum \limits_{k|n} \tau_k b_{\frac n k J} = (\tau *_d b)_{nJ} \quad\text{for all } n\in\mathbb{N}.$$
Since $b$ vanishes outside $\mathbb{N} J$ and $kM\in\mathbb{N} J$ for all $M\in\mathbb{N} J$, also $\tau*_db$ vanishes outside $\mathbb{N} J$. Whence
$$\|\tau*a\|_{\ell_2}=\|\tau*_db\|_{\ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})} \leq \|\tau\|_{\hat \ell_d} \|b\|_{\ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})}=\|\tau\|_{\hat \ell_d} \|a\|_{\ell_2},$$
which shows $\hat \ell_d \subset \hat \ell_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_{\hat \ell_1} \leq \|\cdot\|_{\hat \ell_d}.$

Now let $\tau \in \hat \ell_1$ and $a \in \ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}).$ For $J\in P_d$ define $a^J\in\ell_2$ by $a^J_n:=a_{nJ}$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$. By the above, $(\tau*_da)_{nJ}=\sum_{k|n}\tau_ka_{\frac nkJ}=(\tau*a^J)_n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $J\in P_d$. Using the unique decomposition $K=nJ$ we obtain
$$\|\tau*_da\|_{\ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})}^2 = \sum_{J \in P_d} \sum_{n=1}^\infty (\tau*_da)_{nJ}^2 = \sum_{J \in P_d} \|\tau*a^J\|_{\ell_2}^2 \leq \|\tau\|_{\hat \ell_1}^2 \sum_{J \in P_d} \|a^J\|_{\ell_2}^2 = \|\tau\|_{\hat \ell_1}^2 \sum_{J \in P_d}\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{nJ}^2 = \|\tau\|_{\hat \ell_1}^2 \|a\|_{\ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})}^2.$$
Taking square roots gives $\|\tau*_da\|_{\ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})} \leq \|\tau\|_{\hat \ell_1} \|a\|_{\ell_2( \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0})}$, which shows $\hat \ell_1 \subset \hat \ell_d$ and $\|\cdot\|_{\hat \ell_d} \leq \|\cdot\|_{\hat \ell_1}.$
head: environment

label: CompHLS
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{CompHLS}
For $\tau\in\ell_1$ let $F_\tau(s):=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\tau_n n^{-s}$. By definition, $\hat\ell_1$ consists of the coefficient sequences of the multipliers of the Hilbert space $\mathcal H^2=\{\sum_n a_nn^{-s}:a\in\ell_2\}$ of Dirichlet series, and $\|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_1}$ is the multiplier norm. By \cite[Thm.~3.1]{Seip} the multipliers of $\mathcal H^2$ are exactly the Dirichlet series that converge to bounded analytic functions in $\operatorname{Re}s>0$, and
\[
\|\tau\|_{\hat\ell_1}=\sup_{\operatorname{Re}s>0}|F_\tau(s)|.
\]
Since $F_{\tau^{-1}}=1/F_\tau$, Proposition~\ref{ellhat}(iii) yields the optimal Riesz constants
\[
A=\inf_{\operatorname{Re}s>0}|F_\tau(s)|^2,\qquad B=\sup_{\operatorname{Re}s>0}|F_\tau(s)|^2
\]
of $\mathcal Z^\tau_0$ in $L_2([0,1]^d)_0$, independently of $d$, by Lemma \ref{ellhatd}.

For $d=1$ the restriction to $[0,\frac12]$ followed by the substitution $x=\frac y2$ maps $\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{s_k:k\in\mathbb{N}\}$ isometrically onto $L_2(0,1)$ and $S^\tau_k$ onto $\varphi(ky)$ with $\varphi(y)=\sqrt2\sum_{n}\tau_n\sin(\pi ny)$. Thus, for the sine part, Proposition~\ref{ellhat}(iii) reduces to the Riesz basis criterion of \cite{Seip}. The new aspects of our setting, besides a different method of proof, are the simultaneous treatment of the cosine and the sine part, the multivariate systems indexed by $ \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$, the spaces $L_q([0,1]^d)$ with $q\neq2$, as well as the generalisation to mixed systems in          
the following Subsection \ref{subsect-mixed}.

label: Power series
title: Remark
body_md:
{\textbf{(Holomorphic interpretation).}} \label{Power series} \hypertarget{Power series} Let $\tau \in \ell_1.$ In order to obtain closed expressions for $C^\tau, S^\tau$ we make use of Euler's formula and compute $C^\tau(x) + i S^\tau(x)$ using Taylor series. More generally one may study $\mathcal Z^\tau$ in a complex framework: Consider the power series $$f(z):=\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \tau_n z^n,$$ which converges for all $z \in \mathbb C$ where $|z| \leq 1,$ thus showing that the radius of convergence $\rho$ is at least 1. This allows the evaluation $f(\exp(ix))$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ since  $|\exp(ix)|=1,$ and leads to the formulae $$C^\tau(x) = \sqrt{2}\text{Re}(f(\exp(ix))=\sqrt{2}\frac{f(\exp(ix))+\overline{f(\exp(ix)}} 2 =\sqrt{2} \frac{f(\exp(ix))+f(\exp(-ix))}2,$$ as well as $$S^\tau(x) = \sqrt{2}\text{Im}(f(\exp(ix))=\sqrt{2}\frac{f(\exp(ix))-\overline{f(\exp(ix)}} {2i} = \sqrt{2}\frac{f(\exp(ix))-f(\exp(-ix))}{2i}.$$                                                                                                                                      

Whenever we can find closed expressions for $f,$ we are also able to find analytical expressions for $C^\tau$ and $S^\tau.$ 
If the radius of convergence satisfies $\rho>1,$ then $f$ is holomorphic, whence smooth, on $B_\rho(0).$ Since for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ we have $|\exp(ix)|=1<\rho,$ this shows that $C^\tau$ and $S^\tau$ are even smooth in this case. It is possible that some other insides can be gathered by the means of complex analysis, but we will not look into that.

    Such a power series $f$ can be interpreted as the complex analogue to the operator $T_\tau.$ If additionally $\lambda \in \ell_1$ we can also interpret the operator $T$ from Lemma \ref{MixOp} in terms of holomorphic functions. The reflection operator $R$ behaves similar to the complex conjugation, which                                                       
    however is not an analytic function. Therefore, we need to find a better representation. 
    Since we are only interested in evaluating $\exp(ix)$ the conjugate of which is $\exp(-ix)=\frac{1}{\exp(ix)},$ we will identify $R$ with taking the multiplicative inverse, which is holomorphic on $\mathbb C \backslash \{0\}.$ 
    The analytic analogue to the operator $$T=T_\frac{\tau+\lambda}{2}+T_\frac{\tau-\lambda}{2}^R, \quad (Tg)(x) := \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\tau_k+\lambda_k}{2} g(kx) + \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\tau_k-\lambda_k}{2}g(-kx)$$ then takes the form $$f(z):=\sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\tau_k+\lambda_k}{2}z^k + \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\tau_k-\lambda_k}{2}z^{-k}.$$ Since $\frac{\tau\pm\lambda}{2} \in \ell_1$ the                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
    analytic part converges at least on $\{z \in \mathbb C: |z| \leq 1\}$                                      
    whereas the principal part converges at least on $\{z \in \mathbb C: |z|\geq 1\}.$ Thus, we may evaluate $f(\exp(ix))$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ since $|\exp(ix)|=1$ holds. 
      In order to use the theory from complex analysis we   need to ensure better convergence once more. Let $\rho_g$ be the radius of convergence of the power series $g(z)=\sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\tau_k+\lambda_k}{2}z^k$ and $\rho_h$ the radius of convergence of the power series $\sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\tau_k-\lambda_k}{2}z^k,$ then from the summability of the coefficients we get $\rho_g, \ \rho_h \geq 1.$          
      In case both are strictly greater than $1$, the Laurent series
$f(z)=g(z)+h(1/z)$ with $h(w):=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\tau_k-\lambda_k}{2}w^k$
converges on the open annulus $\{z\in\mathbb C:\rho_h^{-1}<|z|<\rho_g\}$ and defines a holomorphic function there. 
This annulus contains the unit circle and whence $\{\exp(ix):x\in\mathbb{R}\}$.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
For details about the convergence and holomorphity of power series and the expansion into Taylor series see for instance \cite[I §7 and §8, III §4 and §5]{Funktionentheorie} and for details about convergence and holomorphity of Laurent series, see for instance \cite[VI§1]{Funktionentheorie}.
 Lastly,          
 let us point out again that                                                                                                   
 in \cite{Seip} a very similar framework was studied where a connection to Dirichlet series was established, which deepens the connection to holomorphic functions, see Remark \ref{CompHLS}. It is highly likely that a similar procedure can be implemented in our setting.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{DWSC}
    For all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ it holds that $$\mathcal C(2x)= \mathcal C(x)^2 - \mathcal S(x)^2.$$
head: environment
name: \textbf{Double Argument Theorem for $\mathcal C$

title: Proof
body_md:
Since both maps are 1-periodic, it is enough to show equality on [0,1). It holds
$$\mathcal C(x) = \begin{cases}
    1-4x, &\text{ if } 0 \leq x \leq \frac 1 2, \\
    4x-3, &\text{ if } \frac 1 2 < x < 1,
\end{cases}$$ 
as well as 
$$\mathcal S(x) = \begin{cases}
    4x, &\text{ if } 0 \leq x \leq \frac 1 4, \\
    2-4x, &\text{ if } \frac 1 4 < x < \frac 3 4, \\
    4x-4, &\text{ if } \frac 3 4 \leq x < 1.
\end{cases}$$ 
We will distinguish the cases $x \in [0, \frac 1 4], (\frac 1 4, \frac 1 2], (\frac 1 2, \frac 3 4), [\frac 3 4, 1).$ This yields \\
\begin{itemize}
    \item $x \in {[0,\frac 1 4]}: \mathcal C(2x) = 1-8x = (1-4x)^2-(4x)^2 = \mathcal C(x)^2-\mathcal S(x)^2,$
    \item $x \in {(\frac 1 4, \frac 1 2]}: \mathcal C(2x)=8x-3 = (1-4x)^2-(2-4x)^2 = \mathcal C(x)^2-\mathcal S(x)^2,$                                
    \item $x \in {(\frac 1 2, \frac 3 4)}: \mathcal C(2x) = \mathcal C(2x-1) = 5-8x = (4x-3)^2-(2-4x)^2 = \mathcal C(x)^2-\mathcal S(x)^2,$                              
    \item $x \in {[\frac 3 4, 1)}: \mathcal C(2x) = \mathcal C(2x-1) = 8x-7 = (4x-3)^2 - (4x-4)^2 = \mathcal C(x)^2-\mathcal S(x)^2,$                                   
\end{itemize} 
which completes the proof.

label: SKP2
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: \textbf{Scalar products of $\mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal S_\alpha$

title: Proof
body_md:
We will show this theorem using induction over $d \in \mathbb{N}.$

We start with the case $d=1$ for which we are going to use \cite[Lem. 2.1]{4}. We will first prove that $\alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{N}$ are oddly co-linear, if and only if, $\nu_2(\alpha)=\nu_2(\beta),$ where $\nu_2(n)$ denotes the exponent corresponding to 2 in the prime factorisation of $n.$

If $\alpha = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta,$ then $\nu_2(\alpha)=\nu_2(\alpha (2q+1)) = \nu_2(\beta (2p+1)) = \nu_2(\beta).$ On the other hand, if $\nu_2(\alpha)=\nu_2(\beta),$ then $\nu_2(\gcd(\alpha,\beta)) = \nu_2(\alpha)=\nu_2(\beta)$ and $2p+1:= \frac{\alpha}{\gcd(\alpha, \beta)}$ as well as $2q+1:= \frac{\beta}{\gcd(\alpha,\beta)}$ are odd, co-prime numbers such that $\alpha = \frac{ \ \frac{\alpha}{\gcd(\alpha,\beta)} \ }{\frac{\beta}{\gcd(\alpha,\beta)}} \beta = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta.$ Therefore, due to \cite[Lem. 2.1]{4} it holds $$3|\langle \mathcal S_\alpha, \mathcal S_\beta \rangle|=3 \langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal C_\beta \rangle = \frac{\gcd(\alpha,\beta)^4}{\alpha^2\beta^2} = \frac{1}{\left(\frac{\alpha}{\gcd(\alpha,\beta)}\right)^2\left(\frac{\beta}{\gcd(\alpha,\beta)}\right)^2} = \frac{1}{(2p+1)^2(2q+1)^2}$$ and $$\operatorname{sgn}(\langle \mathcal S_\alpha, \mathcal S_\beta \rangle) = - (-1)^{\frac{\alpha + \beta}{2\gcd(\alpha,\beta)}} = (-1)^{\frac 1 2(2p+1+2q+1)-1} = (-1)^{p+q}$$ if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are oddly co-linear. 

Else we have $\nu_2(\alpha) \neq \nu_2(\beta)$ and the scalar products $\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal C_\beta \rangle, \langle \mathcal S_\alpha, \mathcal S_\beta \rangle$ vanish according to \cite[Lem. 2.1]{4}(iii). Similarly all mixed scalar products $\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal S_\beta \rangle$ vanish regardless of $\nu_2(\alpha), \nu_2(\beta)$ because of \cite[Lem. 2.1]{4}(i).

Now assume the assertion is proved for $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\alpha,\beta \in  \mathbb{Z} ^{d+1}_+.$ Given a vector $z \in \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ let $z' \in \mathbb{R}^d$ denote the truncated vector with $z'_j = z_j$ for all $1 \leq j \leq d.$

If $\alpha_{d+1}=0=\beta_{d+1},$ then $\alpha',\beta' \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ as well as $\alpha^Tx=(\alpha')^Tx, \beta x' = (\beta')^Tx'$ hold true for all $x \in [0,1]^{d+1}$ and by Fubini's Theorem it holds $$\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal C_\beta \rangle = \int_{[0,1]^d} \left(\int_{[0,1]} \mathcal C(\alpha^T x) \mathcal C(\beta^T x) \ \mathrm d x_{d+1} \right) \mathrm d x' = \langle \mathcal C_{\alpha'}, \mathcal C_{\beta'}\rangle$$ and analogously for $\mathcal S$ and mixed products. In this case, the theorem directly follows from assumption, as $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are oddly co-linear, if and only if, $\alpha'$ and $\beta'$ are.                                                                              

                                                     
Otherwise we may assume $\alpha_{d+1} \neq 0$ because of symmetry. Let $g:=\gcd(\alpha_d,\alpha_{d+1}),$ then $g \in \mathbb{N}$ and by Euclid's Extended Algorithm we can find integers $u,v \in  \mathbb{Z} $ such that $g=u \alpha_d + v \alpha_{d+1}.$ Let $M$ be the block matrix $$M := \begin{pmatrix}
    1 \!\!\! 1_{d-1} & 0_{d-1,2} \\ 0_{2,d-1} & A 
\end{pmatrix}$$ where $A:=\begin{pmatrix}
        u & v \\ -\frac{\alpha_{d+1}}{g} & \frac{\alpha_d}{g}
    \end{pmatrix}$, then all entries of $M$ are integers and $$\det M = \det A = \frac{u \alpha_d + v \alpha_{d+1}}{g}=1.$$ Further, we set $J:= M \alpha = (\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_{d-1}, g, 0)^T, K := M \beta \in  \mathbb{Z} ^{d+1}_+.$
                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
    Since the integrand is $1$-periodic in every coordinate and $M^T$ is an integer matrix with $\det M^T=1$, the substitution $x\mapsto M^Tx$ maps $[0,1]^{d+1}$ onto a fundamental domain of $ \mathbb{Z} ^{d+1}$, so by the change of variables formula and periodicity the integral does not change. Using $\alpha^TM^Tx=J^Tx$ and $\beta^TM^Tx=K^Tx$ together with Fubini's Theorem we obtain \begin{align*} \int_{[0,1]^{d+1}} \mathcal C(\alpha^T x) \mathcal C(\beta^T x) \mathrm d x &= \int_{[0,1]^{d+1}} \mathcal C(\alpha^T M^T x) \mathcal C(\beta^T M^T x) \mathrm d x \\ &=\int_{[0,1]^{d+1}} \mathcal C(J^T x) \mathcal C(K^T x) \mathrm d x = \int_{[0,1]^d} \mathcal C_{J'} (x') \left(\int_0^1 \mathcal C((K')^T x' +K_{d+1} x_{d+1}) \mathrm d x_{d+1} \right) \mathrm d x'. \end{align*}
    Here, the 1-periodicity of $\mathcal C$ is used, to ensure $\mathcal C(\alpha^T(x+i)) = \mathcal C(\alpha^Tx + \alpha^Ti) = \mathcal C(\alpha^Tx)$ holds for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^d, i \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d$ as $\alpha^Ti = \sum \limits_{j=1}^d\alpha_j i_j \in  \mathbb{Z} .$ Similarly for $\mathcal S$ and mixed products.
    
    Now there are two cases. First consider the case $K_{d+1} \neq 0.$ Then the inner integral vanishes and consequently the scalar product is 0. If $K_{d+1}=0$ however, then the integrand of the inner integral is constant and the value is $\mathcal C((K')^Tx')=\mathcal C_{K'}(x')$ leading to $\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal C_\beta \rangle = \langle \mathcal C_{J'}, \mathcal C_{K'} \rangle.$ Summarised this reads as $$\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal C_\beta \rangle = \begin{cases}
        0, &\text{ if } K_{d+1} \neq 0, \\ \langle \mathcal C_{J'}, \mathcal C_{K'} \rangle, &\text{ if } K_{d+1}=0,
    \end{cases}$$ where $K_{d+1}=\frac{-\alpha_{d+1} \beta_d + \alpha_d \beta_{d+1}}{g} \in  \mathbb{Z} $ as $g=\gcd(\alpha_d, \alpha_{d+1})$ divides $\alpha_d$ and $\alpha_{d+1}$ and consequently the numerator. A completely analogous calculation shows the same result for $\mathcal S$ as well as mixed products. 
    
    We are now able to show the desired formulae. 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item We have seen $\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal S_\beta \rangle = 0,$ if $K_{d+1} \neq 0.$ If $K_{d+1} = 0$ this follows from the induction hypothesis and $\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal S_\beta \rangle = \langle \mathcal C_{J'}, \mathcal S_{K'} \rangle = 0$. Similarly $\langle \mathcal C_\beta, \mathcal S_\alpha \rangle=0.$
        \item Let $\alpha = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta,$ then $J= M \alpha = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} M \beta = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} K$ and $J' = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1}K'$ hold. If one of $\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_{d-1}$ is positive, we have $J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^{d+1}_+$ by definition. Otherwise $\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_{d-1}$ vanish and $g>0$ is the first non-zero entry. In either case it holds $J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^{d+1}_+$ and $K=\frac{2q+1}{2p+1} J \in  \mathbb{Z} ^{d+1}_+$. From $K_{d+1} = \frac{2q+1}{2p+1} J_{d+1} = 0,$ we get $$3 \langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal C_\beta \rangle = 3 \langle \mathcal C_{J'}, \mathcal C_{K'}  \rangle = \frac{1}{(2p+1)^2(2q+1)^2} \quad \text{and} \quad 3 \langle \mathcal S_\alpha, \mathcal S_\beta \rangle = 3 \langle \mathcal S_{J'}, \mathcal S_{K'} \rangle = \frac{(-1)^{p+q}}{(2p+1)^2(2q+1)^2}.$$
        \item Assume now $\alpha, \beta$ not to be oddly co-linear, then there are three cases to be distinguished: 
        \begin{itemize}
        \item[-] If $K_{d+1} \neq 0$ we are done, since the integrals vanish. 
        \item[-] If $K_{d+1}=0$ we again get $\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal C_\beta \rangle = \langle \mathcal C_{J'}, \mathcal C_{K'} \rangle$ and exactly the same for $\mathcal S.$ If $(\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_{d-1}), (\beta_1, ..., \beta_{d-1})$ are not oddly co-linear, then $J'$ and $K'$ are not as well and we again get $\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal C_\beta \rangle=0$ and $\langle \mathcal S_\alpha, \mathcal S_\beta \rangle=0$. 
        \item[-] It remains to show, that in the last case $(\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_{d-1}) = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} (\beta_1, ..., \beta_{d-1})$ and $K_{d+1}=0$ the vectors $J',K'$ are not oddly co-linear. Because the first $d-1$ entries coincide with those from $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we need to prove $g \neq \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} K_d.$
        
                                                                               
        Since $\alpha_{d+1} \neq 0$ was assumed, $\frac{\alpha_d \beta_{d+1}-\alpha_{d+1} \beta_d}{g}=K_{d+1}=0 \text{ implies } \ \alpha_d \frac{\beta_{d+1}}{\alpha_{d+1}}=\beta_d.$
        
        We now distinguish two cases again, namely $\beta_d=0$ and $\beta_d \neq 0.$ First, let us assume $\beta_d$ being zero, then either $\alpha_d=0$ or $\beta_{d+1}=0$ need to hold.
        
        If $\alpha_d=0,$ it follows $\alpha_d = 0 = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \cdot 0 = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta_d.$ We get $\alpha_{d+1} \neq \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta_{d+1}$ because $\alpha, \beta$ are not oddly co-linear. Further, we have $$g=\alpha_{d+1}, \ u=0, \ v=1, \ K_d=u \beta_d + v \beta_{d+1} = \beta_{d+1},$$ yielding $g=\alpha_{d+1}\neq \frac{2p+1}{2q+1}\beta_{d+1}=\frac{2p+1}{2q+1}K_d.$ Second, if $\beta_{d+1}=0,$ then $K_d=0$ and $\frac{2p+1}{2q+1}K_d = 0 \neq g$ ending the proof of the first subcase. 
        
        We may now assume $\beta_d \neq 0$ and rearrange $\alpha_d \frac{\beta_{d+1}}{\alpha_{d+1}}=\beta_d$ to $\alpha_{d+1}=\frac{\beta_{d+1}}{\beta_d}\alpha_d.$
        
        Finally, assume aiming towards a contradiction, that $g=\frac{2p+1}{2q+1}K_d,$ then $$u \alpha_d + v \alpha_{d+1} = g = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} K_d = u \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta_d + v \frac{2p+1}{2q+1}\beta_{d+1} $$ holds, which in turn implies $$ v \left(\alpha_{d+1}-\frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta_{d+1}\right)=u \left(\frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta_d-\alpha_d \right).$$
        Plugging in $\alpha_{d+1}=\frac{\beta_{d+1}}{\beta_d}\alpha_d$ and factoring out $\frac{\beta_{d+1}}{\beta_d},$ leads to $$v \frac{\beta_{d+1}}{\beta_d}\left(\alpha_d-\frac{2p+1}{2q+1}\beta_d\right) = u \left(\frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta_d-\alpha_d\right).$$ Since $\alpha_d = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1}\beta_d$ would imply $\alpha_{d+1} =\frac{\alpha_d}{\beta_d} \beta_{d+1} = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta_{d+1}$ and consequently $\alpha=\frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta,$ we get $\alpha_d-\frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta_d \neq 0$ and may divide both sides by this term. We obtain $v \frac{\beta_{d+1}}{\beta_d} = -u \text{ implying } K_d = u \beta_d + v \beta_{d+1} = 0$ and $g = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1}K_d = 0,$ a contradiction to $g \in \mathbb{N}$, showing $g \neq \frac{2p+1}{2q+1}K_d$ as desired.
        
        Therefore $J',K'$ are not oddly co-linear and $K_{d+1}=0$ implies $$\langle \mathcal C_\alpha, \mathcal C_\beta \rangle = \langle \mathcal C_{J'}, \mathcal C_{K'} \rangle=0 \text{ as well as } \langle \mathcal S_\alpha, \mathcal S_\beta \rangle = \langle \mathcal S_{J'}, \mathcal S_{K'} \rangle=0.$$
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
                                                           
        \end{itemize}
    \end{itemize}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Streichmat}
    Let $k,n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n \geq2, 1 \leq k \leq n.$ Further, let $A,B,C,D\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ such that $D$ is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $D_{ii}$ in $\{-1,1\}.$ We define $C^{\dagger k} \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-1) \times (n-1)}$ to be the matrix gained by deleting the $k$-th row and column from $C,$ that is $$C^{\dagger k}_{ij} = \begin{cases}
    C_{ij} &\text{ if } 1 \leq i,j < k,\\
    C_{i(j+1)} &\text{ if } 1 \leq i < k \leq j \leq n-1,\\
    C_{(i+1)j} &\text{ if } 1 \leq j < k \leq i \leq n-1,\\
    C_{(i+1)(j+1)} &\text{ if } k \leq i,j \leq n-1. \\
\end{cases}$$ 
If $B=DAD,$ then $B^{\dagger k} = D^{\dagger k} A^{\dagger k} D^{\dagger k}.$

label: Gram
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Gram}
Fix $d \in \mathbb{N}.$ Let $M = \{\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_{|M|}\} \subset \{\alpha \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}\}$ be non-empty and finite. Let $G^\mathcal C_M$ be the matrix with $(G^\mathcal C_M)_{ij}:=\langle \mathcal C_{\alpha_i}, \mathcal C_{\alpha_j}\rangle$ and define $G^\mathcal S_M$ analogously. Then $G^\mathcal C_M$ is similar to $G^\mathcal S_M$ and, in particular, their spectra coincide.
head: environment
name: \textbf{Spectra of the truncated Gram matrices

title: Proof
body_md:
First we notice that odd co-linearity defines an equivalence relation on $M.$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Reflexivity: For any $\alpha \in M$ we choose $p=0=q$ to get $\alpha = \frac{1}{1} \alpha.$
        \item Symmetry: Let $\alpha, \beta \in M$ and $\alpha=\frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta,$ then $\beta = \frac{2q+1}{2p+1} \alpha.$
        \item Transitivity: Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in M$ with $\alpha = \frac{2p+1}{2q+1} \beta, \beta = \frac{2r+1}{2s+1} \gamma,$ then $\alpha = \frac{(2p+1)(2r+1)}{(2q+1)(2s+1)}\gamma.$ Numerator and denominator of this fraction are odd as products of odd numbers and simplifying gives co-prime odd numbers as numerator and denominator.
    \end{itemize}

Therefore, $M$ is partitioned into finitely many pairwise disjoint equivalence classes. We may order $M$ in any way and will do so by grouping equivalence classes. To be more precise: 

Let $Q_1=\{\alpha^1_1,  ..., \alpha^1_{|Q_1|}\}, Q_2=\{\alpha^2_1, ..., \alpha^2_{|Q_2|}\}, ..., Q_K=\{\alpha^K_1, ..., \alpha^K_{|Q_K|}\}$ be the equivalence classes arising from odd co-linearity. 
                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                 
Because of Theorem \ref{SKP2}, the resulting matrices are in block-diagonal form and we can write $G^\mathcal C_{M,k} = (\langle \mathcal C_{\alpha_i^k}, \mathcal C_{\alpha_j^k} \rangle)_{i,j \in \{1,..., |Q_k|\}}$ and define $G^\mathcal S_{M,k}$ analogously for all $1 \leq k \leq K$. Then $G^\mathcal C_M$ is similar to $$\begin{pmatrix}
    G^\mathcal C_{M,1} & 0 & ... & 0 \\
    0 & G^\mathcal C_{M,2} & ... & 0 \\ 
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & ... & G^\mathcal C_{M,K}
\end{pmatrix}$$ and all the same for $\mathcal S.$ 

For any equivalence class $Q_k$ and any $l \in \{1, ..., d\},$ $\alpha_l=0$ holds either for all $\alpha \in Q_k$ or for none. Since $\alpha \in  \mathbb{Z} ^d_{+\!\!>0}$ there has to be a smallest $l \in \{1, ..., d\}$ such that $\alpha_l > 0$ for all $\alpha \in Q_k.$

Since the value of $\langle \mathcal C_{\alpha_i^k}, \mathcal C_{\alpha_j^k} \rangle$ only depends on the integers defining the co-linearity scalar which themselves are uniquely determined by the $l$-th entries of the vectors as they are assumed to be co-prime, due to Theorem \ref{SKP2}(i) and (ii), we get $\langle \mathcal C_{\alpha_i^k}, \mathcal C_{\alpha_j^k} \rangle=\langle \mathcal C_{(\alpha_i^k)_l}, \mathcal C_{(\alpha_j^k)_l} \rangle$ and equally for $\mathcal S.$ Thus $G^\mathcal C_{M,k}$ is equal to a block sub-matrix of the one-dimensional Gram matrix and the same is true for $G_{M,k}^\mathcal S.$ These are similar because of \cite[Thm. 2.2]{4} and Lemma \ref{Streichmat}. Therefore, $G_M^\mathcal C$ and $G_M^\mathcal S$ are similar as well, which in particular implies their spectra to coincide. Note that the transformation matrix is again block diagonal, where each block is a diagonal matrix with entries in $\{-1,1\}.$ Therefore, $DG_M^\mathcal C D = G_M^\mathcal S$ holds for some diagonal matrix $D$ with $D_{jj} \in \{-1,1\}$ for all $1 \leq j \leq |M|.$

\label{Rdbasis}
    Let $q \in (1,\infty)$ and $d \in \mathbb{N}.$ The system $\mathcal R_d$ forms a Schauder basis of $L_q([0,1]^d).$ In case of $q=2,$ it forms a Riesz basis where $A=\frac 2 3$ and $B=\frac 3 2.$

name: \textbf{Basis properties of $\mathcal R_d$

title: Proof
body_md:
We will first prove the formula $\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{|\mu(2n-1)|}{(2n-1)^2}=\frac{12}{\pi^2},$ where $\mu$ is the Möbius function. Let $L: \mathbb{N} \to \{-1,1\}$ be the Liouville function, that is introduced in \cite[Ch. 2.12]{Numertheory}. There, it is shown, that $L$ is completely multiplicative and that it is the Dirichlet inverse of $|\mu|$. 
    
    Since $L$ and $|\mu|$ are bounded by 1 the Dirichlet series $\zeta(s):=\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^s}$, $\xi(s):=\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{L(n)}{n^s}$ and $\eta(s):=\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{|\mu(n)|}{n^s}$ converge for all $s \in \mathbb C$ with $\text{Re}(s)>1.$ In \cite[Ex. 6 in Ch. 11.4]{Numertheory} the formula $\eta(s)=         
    \frac{\zeta(s)}{\zeta(2s)}$ for all $s \in \mathbb C$ such that $\text{Re}(s)>1$ is derived. Moreover, for all $s \in \mathbb C$ such that $\text{Re}(s)>1$ it holds $\xi(s) \eta(s)=\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(L*|\mu|)(n)}{n^s}=\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{e(n)}{n^s}=1$ and $\xi(s)=\frac 1 {\eta(s)}=         
    \frac{\zeta(2s)}{\zeta(s)}.$ 
 Now $\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{|\mu(n)|}{n^2}=         
 \eta(2)=\frac{\zeta(2)}{\zeta(4)}=\frac{15}{\pi^2}$ follows. Further, \begin{align*}\frac{15}{\pi^2}=\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{|\mu(n)|}{n^2}&=\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{|\mu(2n)|}{(2n)^2}+\sum \limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{|\mu(2n-1)|}{(2n-1)^2} \\ &=\sum \limits_{n \in 2\mathbb{N}} \frac{|\mu(2n)|}{(2n)^2}+\sum \limits_{n \in 2\mathbb{N}-1} \frac{|\mu(2n)|}{(2n)^2}+\sum \limits_{n \in 2\mathbb{N}-1} \frac{|\mu(n)|}{n^2} \\ &= \frac{|\mu(2)|}{2^2}\sum \limits_{n \in 2\mathbb{N}-1} \frac{|\mu(n)|}{n^2}+\sum \limits_{n \in 2\mathbb{N}-1} \frac{|\mu(n)|}{n^2}=\frac 5 4 \sum \limits_{n \in 2\mathbb{N}-1} \frac{|         
 \mu(n)|}{n^2} \end{align*} holds true, 
          
 because $2^2 \mid 2n$ for even $n$ implies $\mu(2n)=0$ in this case, and for odd $n$ the multiplicativity of $\mu$ together with $\gcd(2,n)=1$ yields $|\mu(2n)|=|\mu(2)|\,|\mu(n)|=|\mu(n)|$.
                                                                                     
 Thus, the desired formula is achieved after division by $\frac 5 4.$

    By \cite[p.166]{mathcalCS} we see that it holds $$\sqrt 3 \mathcal C = \sqrt 2 \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac{4 \sqrt 6}{\pi^2} \frac{1}{(2k-1)^2}c_{2k-1}=C^\tau \quad \text{ and } \quad \sqrt 3 \mathcal S=\sqrt 2 \sum \limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac{4 \sqrt 6}{\pi^2} \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{(2k-1)^2} s_{2k-1}=S^\lambda,$$ where $$\tau_k:= \begin{cases}
        0, &\text{ if } k \text{ is even, } \\ \frac{4\sqrt 6}{\pi^2} \frac 1 {k^2}, &\text{ if } k \text{ is odd,}
    \end{cases}$$ and          
    $\lambda_{2k-1}=(-1)^{k+1}\tau_{2k-1}$. Both sequences $\tau$ and $\lambda$ satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{Basiscrit}(ii) and Theorem \ref{MixedZystems}.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
In particular, using Theorem \ref{Basiscrit}(ii)  with $\tau_1=\lambda_1=\frac{4\sqrt6}{\pi^2}$, $\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}=\|\lambda\|_{\ell_1}=\frac{4\sqrt6}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{8}=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}$ and $\|\mu\cdot\tau\|_{\ell_1}=\|\mu\cdot\lambda\|_{\ell_1}=\frac{48\sqrt6}{\pi^4}$ we obtain
$$A_\tau=A_\lambda=\frac 1 {\|\tau^{-1}\|_{\ell_1}^2}=\frac{|\tau_1|^4}{\|\mu\cdot\tau\|_{\ell_1}^2}=\frac{(4\sqrt6)^4\pi^{-8}}{(48\sqrt6)^2\pi^{-8}}=\frac23,
\quad \text{ and } \quad B_\tau=B_\lambda=\|\tau\|_{\ell_1}^2=\frac32 .$$
Theorem \ref{MixedZystems} with $k_0=1$ now yields $A=\min\{1,\frac23\}=\frac23$ and $B=\max\{1,\frac32\}=\frac32$.
